title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Mining | MPI (US)
description: Mag particle inspection for US mines and quarries: truck frames, boom welds, wheel parts, hooks, pins and shafts. Mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Mining Equipment and Mineral Plants in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) on mining machinery across the United States. We look for surface and near-surface cracks in welds, pins, shafts, hooks and cast or forged parts on haul trucks, shovels, draglines, crushers, mills and conveyors. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. To start, request an MT inspection quote with the component list and the site address.

Why mine equipment cracks, and where magnetic particle testing looks

Most structural failures on mining equipment begin as a fatigue crack at a stress concentration: a weld toe, a pin bore, a keyway corner, a change in section. Loading is cyclic and often shock-loaded, so a crack that is shallow today may be through the wall in a few months of production. Magnetic particle inspection is the method built for exactly that kind of defect. It reveals cracks that open to the surface, and those lying just under it, in ferromagnetic steel, and it does so in minutes on the actual part, with a result you can see.

The principle is simple. We magnetize the part. Where a crack interrupts the magnetic field, flux leaks out of the surface and holds fine iron particles, drawing the crack as a sharp line. Because the line appears right on the weld or the pin, there is no interpretation of a screen; the inspector and the maintenance planner are looking at the same thing. For defects that sit deeper in the section, the companion method is covered on the page for ultrasonic testing for mining.

Components where MT earns its place

  • Welded frames and booms. Weld toes on haul truck main rails, body hinge brackets, shovel and dragline boom chords and lacing, and crane and hoist structures in mine shops.
  • Pins, bushing seats and bores. Boom foot pins, equalizer pins, sheave pins and the lugs they pass through. Cracks run from the bore edge or the thread relief.
  • Wheel and axle parts. Hub flanges, rim components, spindles and fasteners on large mining trucks. Wheel end parts are safety critical, and MT on removed parts shows cracks that a visual check will not.
  • Lifting gear. Hooks, shackles, lifting lugs, spreader beams and the maintenance cranes that lift liners and motors. These are covered in the job page for magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment.
  • Castings and forgings. Bucket adapters, hinge blocks, gear blanks, crusher frames and forged shafts, handled in more detail on magnetic particle inspection of castings and forgings.
  • Drive shafts and pulley shafts. Keyway corners, shoulders and thread roots, where a transverse fatigue crack starts.

Where we work in the US mining regions

Mines sit far from cities, so planning begins from the city a crew travels through. Atlantis has no office near the site; technicians are mobilized to the mine for the scope. The MT pages for these cities describe the local industry and the codes in more detail.

  • Magnetic particle testing in Tucson covers the Arizona copper belt and the repair shops that rebuild its trucks.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Phoenix serves central Arizona mines and the fabricators supplying them.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Salt Lake City is the hub for Utah copper and industrial minerals.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Minneapolis reaches Minnesota iron range plants, where cold winter air makes dry-powder methods attractive.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Birmingham reflects Alabama coal, foundries and machine shops.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Anchorage supports Alaska mines and gravel operations.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Spokane covers northern Rockies and Inland Northwest metals mines.
  • Magnetic particle testing in El Paso and Albuquerque serve southwestern and New Mexico operations.

Standards and who accepts the result

The Mine Safety and Health Administration regulates mines through 30 CFR Parts 56 and 57 (metal and nonmetal) and Parts 75 and 77 (coal). Those rules demand safe equipment but do not write an MT procedure. Our procedures follow ASTM E709, the guide for magnetic particle testing, and ASTM E1444 for the practice, with ASME Section V Article 7 as the usual reference for the method. For welded equipment the acceptance code is normally AWS D14.3 (earthmoving, construction, agricultural and industrial equipment), AWS D1.1 for structures, or the equipment manufacturer's repair standard. Cranes and hooks fall under the ASME B30 series, with B30.10 covering hooks, and OSHA applies to overhead and gantry cranes in shop buildings.

The acceptance criteria belong to the owner, the engineer of record or the maker. Our report compares each indication against the named criterion; whether a crack is repaired, ground out or the part scrapped is your decision. Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II performing and interpreting the test and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. A plain-language guide is at the complete MT guide, and the code article is ASME Section V Article 7 explained.

Technique choices for field mining work

The method itself is straightforward. The details decide whether a crack is found.

  • Yoke or prods. For most field work we use an AC electromagnetic yoke, which finds surface cracks and can be moved quickly along a weld. Its lifting force is checked against the lift limit in the procedure, and we read particle patterns with the yoke placed twice at right angles so cracks in either direction show.
  • Dry powder or wet suspension. Dry colored powder copes with rough and warm surfaces but blows away in open-pit wind, so shelter is often needed. Wet visible suspension from an aerosol gives finer sensitivity on clean weld toes. Fluorescent particles need dim light and an ultraviolet lamp, so we use a shelter or work at the shop.
  • Surface condition. Heavy rust, scale, grease and thick paint reduce sensitivity. Thin coatings are acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated through them; otherwise we ask for blasting or grinding at the inspection location.
  • Contrast. Black particles on a thin white contrast paint stand out on pit-weathered grey steel.
  • Demagnetizing. Rotating shafts and bearing seats are demagnetized after testing so steel debris does not collect on them. The procedure states the acceptable residual field.

What magnetic particle testing finds and misses

MT, PT and UT on mining parts
PartMT resultWhen to use another method
Truck frame weld toeShows open cracks and tight onesUT if the crack may lie below the surface in thick plate
Hook or pinShows surface cracks, laps, seamsUT for depth in large cross sections
Austenitic manganese steel partDoes not work, the alloy is not magneticPT for surface cracks, see the PT page
Stainless piping or aluminum castingDoes not workPT for surface defects

MT does not tell you how deep a crack is, and it does not see flaws buried more than a short distance below the surface. A very coarse surface or thick coating will hide fine cracks. We state the limits at quote stage. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and techniques outside MT, PT and UT are not part of this service.

Mine access, conditions and permits

Before anyone enters a mine, the operator must make sure contractors have the right hazard training, normally under 30 CFR Part 46 or Part 48 depending on the operation. We arrange this ahead of the visit and ask for the safety contact when you inquire. Typical practical points for MT work at mines include shelter or tents against wind and dust, lighting for visible particles, scaffolds or lifts for tall structures, and clean power for the yoke or a portable generator. Truck and shovel inspections are best done at a scheduled shutdown with the machine parked and locked out, and the surfaces already cleaned by the shop. We do not promise a crew arrival time; we agree dates with your planner.

What the MT report contains

You receive component identification, location and a sketch of each examined area, the procedure and revision, the equipment (yoke or coil, particle type, lifting force check, light intensity for visible work), the technician and level, the surface condition and cleaning, and each indication with position, length and orientation. For every indication the report states accept or reject against the named code, and photographs are included where possible. The Level III reviews and signs. If the part is later repaired, the same report format covers the re-examination after the weld repair.

What to send for a quote

  • List of parts and equipment with model numbers, locations and photographs.
  • Material, thickness and any coating on the surfaces to be examined.
  • Acceptance code or maker standard and the prior inspection history, if any.
  • Where the work happens: in a shop, at the pit, or inside a plant, and who supplies access equipment.
  • Site address, MSHA training requirements, permits and the shutdown window.

Training your own staff in MT

If your mine shop wants in-house capability for routine checks, the Atlantis MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training are built on SNT-TC-1A, with practice on the magnetic particle simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so the training feeds your written practice. For outside review of procedures we offer NDT technical procedure development. Compare methods in MT versus PT if you are choosing between the two for a new part. The national page magnetic particle testing gives the general overview. The company management system behind this work is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can MT be used on manganese steel crusher liners?
faq.a: No. Austenitic manganese steel is not ferromagnetic, so it does not hold a magnetic field and MT will not show cracks. Penetrant testing is the usual method for surface cracks on those parts, and our penetrant testing for mining page explains how it is done on liners and teeth.

faq.q: How do you inspect a haul truck frame for fatigue cracks?
faq.a: We clean the weld toes and corners, apply contrast paint, magnetize with a yoke in two directions, and spray the particles on. Cracks show as lines on the weld toe or corner. The report lists each indication with position, length and orientation, and compares it to the acceptance criterion you specify.

faq.q: Is fluorescent or visible particle testing better for mining?
faq.a: Visible particles are more practical at the pit because they need no darkness. Fluorescent particles are more sensitive but require a dim shelter and a UV lamp, so we use them in the shop or inside a tent. The procedure states which is used and why.

faq.q: Does MSHA require magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: MSHA requires equipment to be maintained safely, but it does not list MT as a required method. The owner or the equipment manufacturer sets the inspection requirement. We perform the work and report to your acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Can you test through paint on mining equipment?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded paint is acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated through it, but thick coatings reduce sensitivity. We usually ask the site to remove paint locally at the weld toes and pin bores. The report records what coating was on the surface.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT on a shovel boom?
faq.a: Send boom drawings or weld maps, photographs, the maker's inspection requirements if any, the criteria you want applied, access arrangements and the site address with the safety training the mine requires. A list of the welds and pins to be examined is enough to begin, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you also test for subsurface cracks?
faq.a: MT finds cracks at the surface and just below it. For deeper flaws in thick plate, shafts or forgings, ultrasonic testing is the better method, and we often combine the two on the same component when the risk justifies it.

faq.q: Who decides whether a cracked part is repaired or scrapped?
faq.a: You or your engineer do. Our report states the indications and compares them to the acceptance criteria. Repair procedures, repair welding and return-to-service decisions belong to the owner, the maker or a qualified welding engineer. We can re-examine after the repair.

faq.q: Do you perform radiography on mining equipment?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, since it requires a radioactive materials license. Where a project needs it, the owner engages a licensed contractor. We can review the radiographs as an ASNT Level III service if you want an independent look.
